explanation: Schedule 11 rickshaw trips and 11 ox cart trips, which together move 880 coconuts, the most the model allows. The pollution rule is the constraint that limits the plan: rickshaw trips cannot exceed ox cart trips, so the two counts are held equal. The $200 budget is not the bottleneck, since $2 of it stays unspent.

Stock no dining tables and order 133 chairs. This gives a profit of $9,975, the most the model allows under its rules. Floor space, the chair-share rule, and the capital limit all still have room, with 234 sq ft of floor space, 39.9 units of chair-share margin, and $50 of capital left over. Those leftover amounts mean the store is not running at full capacity, so the whole-number requirement (you can't buy part of a chair or table) is what limits the result most. Because chairs earn less per item but use less space and capital, the model finds that filling the store with chairs beats any mix that includes tables.

The bakery should make 20 chocolate cakes and 30 vanilla cakes each day. Together these bring in a profit of $530. Vanilla cakes are the more profitable of the two, so they are made up to the 30 that customers will buy, and the rest of the daily capacity goes to chocolate. The limit is the 50-cake daily production capacity, which is completely used, and the vanilla demand of 30, which is also fully used. Chocolate demand is not the constraint, since 30 chocolate cakes of demand go unmet, but the staffing limit means the bakery can't make more.

Run 48 magazine ads and 8 flyers, and no billboard ads. This is expected to reach 520,000 viewers, the most the model allows. The flyer limit of 8 is the binding constraint, so it is what stops the plan from reaching more viewers. The budget has $400 left unused, and the billboard and magazine share rules still have room (slack of 56 and 39.6), so they are not what holds the result back. The model does not give shadow prices, so it cannot say how much more the budget or the flyer limit would be worth.

Make about 10.11 units of peppers and 8.72 units of tomatoes, which gives the cheapest paste at a cost of about $124.47. This mix exactly meets the minimum of 130 spice units and 90 flavor units, with nothing left over. Each extra unit of required spice would raise the cost by about $0.57, and each extra unit of required flavor by about $0.55. The plan is limited by those two minimums, so any stricter requirement makes the paste more expensive.

Make 40 two-piece suits and 28 three-piece suits. This plan gives the highest profit the store can reach under its limits, $46,400. Stitching time is completely used, and the store is exactly at its minimum of 40 two-piece suits, so these two limits stop the plan from earning more. Measuring time has 54 hours left over, so it is not what holds the plan back. Making more suits would require more stitching time, and the model's rules do not allow that.

Produce only the Premium grade, about 11.67 tons per month, and make no Standard or Plus alloy. This plan brings in a profit of about $64,167 per month. Zinc ore is the bottleneck: all 35 tons are used, while about 80 tons of iron ore sit unused, so extra iron would add nothing. Each additional ton of zinc ore would raise profit by about $1,833, so zinc supply is the main limit on earnings.

Prepare 80 containers of diced onions and 60 containers of diced carrots. This gives a total profit of $1000, the most possible within the given time limits. Both peeling time (2000 minutes) and cutting time (2500 minutes) are fully used, so these two resources are what limit production. Making more of either item would require more of at least one of these resources, which the kitchen doesn't have.

Produce 7 foldable phones and 43 regular phones each week. This plan brings in the highest possible weekly profit, $16,400. The software section's 150 hours are fully used, so it is the limit: adding any phone would require more software time. The hardware section has 1 hour to spare, so it is not what limits production.

Produce 2,000 Gilgamesh Supreme monitors and no Aleph 3 monitors. This yields the highest possible profit, $5,000,000. Assembly time is the bottleneck: all 5,000 available hours are used, so no more monitors can be made without more assembly time. Packaging is not the limit, since 1,500 of its 2,500 allowed hours go unused.

The factory should make about 10.29 kg of rice and 33.82 kg of corn, which yields a maximum profit of about $1,051.47. Machine work and sun-resting time are both used up completely, so they are the bottlenecks. Each extra machine hour would add about $4.71 to profit, and each extra hour of sun-resting time about $1.47. Human labor is not a constraint, with about 45.59 hours left unused, so adding more of it would not help. These results assume the stated hourly requirements and profits are exact and that the factory can produce fractional kilograms.

David should buy 2 bottles of coconut water and 1 bottle of blue energade, for a total cost of $11, the lowest cost that meets all his requirements. This mix satisfies his minimum needs for magnesium and calcium exactly, and it gives him 5 units more potassium than the minimum of 15. Magnesium and calcium are both fully used, so this plan has no spare room on those two. The solution assumes whole bottles and current prices, and the model does not report how the cost would change if his requirements shifted.

Plant no strawberries and devote all 120 acres... no, plant 50 acres of watermelons and leave the rest of the farmland unplanted. This earns the maximum profit of $25,000. The spraying days are the bottleneck: every watermelon acre needs 2 spraying days, so the 100 days available are fully used. Each extra spraying day would add about $250 in profit, but George's land (70 acres unused) and watering days (140 unused) are not limiting anything.

Produce no gel nail paints and 96 acrylic nail paints each month. This gives a total monthly profit of $19,200. Mixing time is the bottleneck: all 480 available mixing hours are used, so it stops you from making more. Raw material hours (98 unused) and packing hours (289.2 unused) are not the limit.

Put **$3,000 in GICs** and **$7,000 in the index ETF**. This mix earns the maximum expected return of **$585** for the year and meets both the $4,000 minimum ETF requirement and the 30% safe-GIC requirement. The plan is limited by two constraints: the full $10,000 is already used, and the GIC floor is exactly met, so the $3,000 in low-yield GICs is what holds the return down. Each extra dollar of budget would add about $0.075 in return, but each extra dollar required in GICs would cost about $0.055. The ETF minimum has $3,000 of room, so it does not limit the plan.

Both the dye and the filler are fully used, so they are the limits: one more kg of dye would add about $14.62 in profit, and one more kg of filler would add about $5.38.

The stand should make 20 pitchers of lemonade and no brownies each day. That yields a profit of $400, the most the model allows. John's 10 hours are fully used, and that is what limits production, while William has 4 of his 8 hours left over. Brownies take twice as much of John's time per unit as lemonade and earn less per unit, so the model doesn't choose them. The result also assumes the stated hour requirements and profits are accurate for each day.

Produce 1 economical phone and 12 premium phones per week. This plan earns a profit of $4950, and it uses the hardware section's hours almost completely, leaving only 1 hour unused. The software section has 61 hours to spare, so it is not a constraint on this plan. The limit is that the hardware section is nearly full, so any extra production would need more hardware hours, and the model does not say how much extra profit each additional hour would bring.

explanation: The plant should make 16 kg of ham and 220 kg of bacon per week, which uses all 2000 machine minutes and fills the bacon limit. This gives a weekly profit of $2960. The machine time and the bacon capacity are both fully used, so they are what limit profit. Each extra machine minute would add about $1.33 to profit, and each extra kg of bacon allowed would add the same amount. The ham limit is not a constraint, since 184 kg of ham capacity goes unused.

Hire no UI designers and staff the team with 50 software engineers, for a weekly wage bill of $100000. This is the cheapest way to reach the 50-worker minimum, since engineers cost less per week. Only the total headcount requirement is binding. The engineer minimum is exceeded by 40, the experience ratio has 150 to spare, and the wage bill is $100000 under its $200000 limit, so none of those rules restrict the answer. The result depends on the current wages and headcount targets, and the analysis gives no shadow prices, so it does not show how much the cost would change if those limits moved.

The factory should make no bike tires and 100 car tires. This earns the maximum profit of $2000. The manufacturing machine is the bottleneck: it runs for the full 600 minutes, so making more car tires would require more machine time than the factory has. The air-filling station still has 50 minutes unused, so it is not what limits production.

The lowest-cost plan is to make 1,200 raincoats and no umbrellas. This meets the weekly requirement of at least 1,200 items at a total production cost of $8,400. Raincoats are cheaper per unit ($7 versus $12), so the plan uses only raincoats. The 1,200-item requirement is fully used, which is what limits the plan, while the 70-hour machine requirement has 290 hours of slack and is not a constraint on this plan. No shadow prices were provided, so the model does not say how much the cost would change if the weekly minimum changed.

Make 38 regular packages and 39 premium packages. This plan treats 193 people, the most possible under the rules. The rule that regular packages must be fewer than premium packages is the one that holds the plan back, since it is fully used. The medicinal herbs have 130 units left over, the drying machine has 20 seconds left over, and the minimum of 15 regular packages is exceeded by 23, so those resources and requirements are not what limit the result.

Use no drones and 32 couriers. This delivers exactly the required 800 packages (each courier moves 25 per hour), and 32 is the smallest total the model allows. The package requirement is the only constraint that is fully used, and $660 of the $1,300 budget goes unspent. The model doesn't give shadow prices, so it can't say how the result would change if the package target moved. Because the plan depends entirely on couriers, it also assumes couriers are always available at that scale.

Make 50 anti-inflammatory containers and 62 pain-killing containers. This plan needs 324 units of water, the smallest amount that meets all the requirements. The minimum of 50 anti-inflammatory containers is the constraint that sets the plan, while 914 units of antibiotics are still unused, so antibiotics are not the bottleneck. The 55% pain-killing requirement is also met, with a small margin of 0.4. The solution doesn't report shadow prices, so it doesn't say how much the water need would change if the minimum of 50 were raised or lowered.

Send 10 cars and 8 trucks. This uses 212 units of gas, the lowest total that meets the delivery target and the rule that cars outnumber trucks. Neither constraint is fully used: the flower requirement has 2 units of spare capacity, and the car-over-truck rule has 1 unit of room beyond its minimum. The model doesn't report shadow prices, so it doesn't show how much the gas total would change if the delivery target or the car-truck rule were adjusted. The answer also assumes whole vehicles only, so it applies only to those exact counts.

The child should have **1 serving of fruit and 8 servings of juice per week**, which gives the lowest possible sugar intake of **121 units**. This plan meets the mineral requirement with only **1 unit to spare**, so the mineral target is nearly the limiting factor. Hydration has **11 units** of extra margin, and the rule that juice servings be at least twice the fruit servings has **6 servings** of margin. No constraint is exactly fully used, so the plan is limited mainly by the tight mineral target, and it would need to be rechecked if the nutritionist's targets or the food contents change.

Take 2 servings of sleeping pills and 2 servings of sleep supplement. This gives the lowest sugar total the model allows, 7 units. It produces 11 units of sleepiness, 1 more than the 10 required, and 1.8 units of discomfort, 0.7 below the 2.5 limit. No constraint is fully used, so the sleepiness and discomfort limits both still have some room. The plan works only because the servings are whole numbers, and the model gives no shadow prices to show how much the limits themselves are worth.

Make 2 salmon lunches and 7 bison burgers. This gives the lowest fat intake the model allows, 107 grams. The carbohydrate requirement of 180 grams is exactly met, so carbs are the constraint that limits the plan. The protein target is exceeded by 80 grams, and the 25% cap on salmon lunches has 0.25 units of room left, so neither one is holding the plan back. Because the answer uses whole meals, it is a practical plan rather than a fractional one.

Make no batches of mixture A and about 42.86 batches of mixture B. This gives the largest total eruption, about 171.43 units. Vinegar is the limiting ingredient: all 300 units are used, so it caps the result. Each extra unit of vinegar would add about 0.57 units of eruption, while the leftover baking soda (about 28.57 units) and garbage allowance (about 17.14 units) would not help on their own.

constraints.name: medium bags at least 3 times specialty bags

explanation: Send 12 specialty delivery bags and 38 medium bags, which together can deliver 410 orders, the most the rules allow. The 50-bag total is the limit that matters most, since it is fully used and caps how many orders can go out. The rule requiring at least three medium bags per specialty bag is met with 2 bags to spare, so it isn't what holds the total down. The stock limits of 45 medium bags and 60 specialty bags are not reached, so they don't restrict this plan.

Set up 13 large production lines and no small ones, which is the cheapest option in terms of line count. This gives the smallest possible number of lines, 13, while still meeting the daily demand of at least 6300 sets, which is exceeded by 200 sets. It leaves 97 of the 435 employees unassigned. Because neither the employee limit nor the demand requirement is fully used, the plan is not held back by either one, and the model does not provide shadow prices to show how the result would change if those limits moved.

explanation: The best plan is to use no small trucks and assign all 208 acres to large logging trucks, which transports 1456 units of wood. The carbon dioxide cap of 5200 units is the binding limit, so it stops any further gain, while 242 acres of land and 704 units of gasoline remain unused. Each extra unit of carbon dioxide allowed would add about 0.28 units of wood transported, so loosening the pollution cap is the only change that would increase output. This result depends only on the land, gasoline, and carbon dioxide limits in the model, and it assumes the per-acre figures hold.

Use **15 commercial planes** and **30 private planes**, which keeps private planes at exactly twice the commercial count as required. This fleet uses **45 planes** in total, the fewest that can meet the traveler requirement under the twice-as-many rule. The ratio rule is the binding limit: it fixes the mix, so the airport cannot swap in more commercial planes to cut the count further. The traveler requirement has 100 travelers of spare capacity, so the fleet slightly exceeds the 3500 needed. The solution does not report shadow prices, so the model does not say how the plane count would change if the requirement or the ratio changed.

The company should transport 20 large cans and 47 small cans, for 67 cans in total, which is the fewest that meets all the requirements. The minimum of 20 large cans for the basic colours is the binding requirement, so it sets the number of large cans. The paint requirement is comfortably exceeded, with 94 litres more than the 120-litre minimum, so it is not what limits the plan. The 30% cap on large cans is also met, with a small margin of 0.1 in the constraint's terms, so it is nearly the limit as well.

Order **100 boxes and 300 buckets**, which transports **3,400 units** of strawberries, the most the rules allow. The main limit is the requirement that buckets be at least three times the number of boxes, which is exactly met, so it is what caps the total. The 650-container limit still has 250 containers of room, and the minimum of 25 boxes is exceeded by 75, so neither is holding the answer back.

The supermarket should buy 10 ABC refrigerators and 5 XYZ refrigerators, for a total of 15 units, which is the fewest that meets every requirement. This mix stores at least 1500 items while staying within the 55 kWh electricity limit. The XYZ minimum of 5 is the only constraint fully used, so it is what currently holds the count down, and the energy limit still has 20 kWh to spare. Item storage exceeds the 1500-item requirement by 100 items, and the ABC count is 2 above its minimum of 8, so the plan has some room but is not padded much.

Schedule 115 tonometer tests and 112 "puff of air" tests, for 227 patients in total. This plan uses nearly all of the 8 office hours, leaving only 0.01 hours unused. It also meets both scheduling rules: tonometer tests exceed the required margin over puff tests by 2, and puff tests are 82 above the minimum of 30. The main limit is time, since the office hours are almost fully used, so the plan can't grow without more hours. Note that the model counts eye-pressure checks, not the temperature checks mentioned in the question.

Schedule **50 dentist shifts** and **80 oral hygienist shifts**, for a total of **130 shifts**, the fewest that still meets the requirements. This covers the 1,000 hours of labour the firm needs and stays within the $65,000 budget. Both the hours and the budget are used up exactly, so the plan has no spare capacity in either. The plan is also limited by those two constraints: any change that adds hours or spends more would need more money or more shifts. The minimum of 20 dentist shifts is not what limits the plan, since 50 dentist shifts are scheduled, which leaves 30 above the minimum.

Schedule 26 bike trips and 11 car trips. This gives the lowest total of 1,370 minutes of trip time while meeting the delivery and pollution requirements. The order requirement is met with 12 orders to spare, and the bike-share rule is met with a small margin of 0.1. No constraint is fully used, and no shadow prices were reported, so the model does not show how much the total time would change if a requirement were tightened. Because the trip counts must be whole numbers, this schedule is the best available whole-number plan, not just a rounded version of an ideal one.

The company should schedule 44 logging truck trips and 43 lumber carrier vessel trips. This moves the required lumber at the lowest total cost, $54,000. The plan uses the rule that trucks must exceed vessels by at least one, and that rule is exactly met, so it is the main limit on the solution. The lumber requirement is also satisfied, with 2,000 lbs more than the 300,000 lbs minimum, so the plan does not waste any trips beyond that surplus. Because the company must have one more truck trip than vessel trips, any change to the vessel count would also force a change to the truck count.

Hire 46 full-time tutors and 208 assistant tutors, for a total of 254 staff, the fewest that still covers the 1200 required teaching hours. This mix meets the Christmas-break demand exactly, with no hours to spare. The budget is not fully used, leaving $140 unspent. The plan is limited by the budget and the hours requirement: the hours target is fully met, and any change in staffing would need to keep the total at 1200 hours while staying within the $55000 budget.

The patient should drink 17 protein shakes and 51 glasses of milk, which meets the protein and milk-preference rules at the lowest sugar intake the model allows, 306 grams. The protein requirement and the milk-preference rule are both exactly met, so this plan leaves no room to drink less of either. The calcium requirement is exceeded by 216 units, so calcium is not what limits the plan. The model does not give shadow prices, so it cannot say how much the sugar total would change if the protein target or the milk ratio changed.

Use **17 truck trips and 10 boat trips**. This is the lowest-pollution plan that still moves the required 1000 units, with a total of **1960** units of pollution. No limit is fully used, so the plan has room to spare: it moves 10 units more than required, the boat share sits 0.8 below its 40% cap, and it has 7 more truck trips than the minimum of 10. Because none of the constraints is binding, the solver reports no shadow prices, so the model doesn't show how much the pollution total would change if any limit were relaxed. The answer is also only as good as the inputs: it assumes the pollution per trip and the capacities stay fixed and that trips can only be whole numbers.

Run 0 force experiments and 7 hydraulics experiments. This gives the maximum total excitement of 35 within the lab's limits. No resource is completely used up: 41 units of solid, 43 units of gas, and 1 unit of the 15-unit heat allowance are left over. The heat allowance is the tightest of the three, so it is the main constraint on the plan, but the report doesn't say how much extra excitement one more unit of heat would add.

The athlete should drink 27 scoops of chocolate powder shakes and 56 scoops of vanilla powder shakes. This gives her a total of 1,548 grams of protein over the month, the most possible within her rules. The sugar limit of 500 grams is completely used up, so it is the main constraint holding the plan back. The "at least twice as much vanilla" rule and the "at least 2 chocolate scoops" rule are both met with room to spare, so they are not what limits the result.

Run Analyzer 3000 for 22 hours and QuickAnalytics for 14 hours. This produces the lowest possible total heat, 140 units, while analyzing at least 1,000 water samples and 800 dirt samples. Both requirements are met exactly, with no extra capacity left over. Each additional water sample required would add about 0.1 units of heat, and each additional dirt sample about 0.05 units, so these two sample requirements are what limit how low the heat can go.

constraints.name: hardcover at least three times paperback

explanation: The team should build **1 toy car and 6 toy trucks**, which raises a total of **$240**. Wheels are the limiting resource: all 40 are used, so no more toys can be made without more wheels. The team still has 8 units of wood left over, and the car limit and the "more trucks than cars" rule are not binding. The data don't include shadow prices, so this result can't tell you how much extra money another wheel would add.

Hire 24 architects and 23 drafters each week. Together they complete 71 projects per week, the most the budget allows under the supervision rule. The weekly cost is about $99,600, leaving $400 of the $100,000 budget unused, which isn't enough to add another drafter or architect. The main limit is the rule that architects must outnumber drafters: here the gap is exactly one, so that rule is what caps the team size.

Use 5 shuttle buses and 43 taxis. This moves at least 250 workers for the lowest total cost, $2,250. Both the worker requirement and the 5-bus limit are fully used, so the plan has no spare capacity and no slack in either constraint. The plan depends on the current limits: it already uses the maximum allowed shuttle buses, so any change in worker numbers or bus availability would require re-running the model.

The plant should process **20 batches of liquid waste and 10 batches of solid waste**. This serves **230 people**, the maximum possible under the constraints. The main limits are the 2-to-1 rule between liquid and solid batches and the storage cap of 10 solid batches, which are both fully used. Disinfectant and bacteria are not the bottleneck: 650 units of disinfectant and 450 units of bacteria would remain unused.

Use the van for all 20 trips and make no truck trips. This gives the lowest total travel time, 200 hours. The 20-trip requirement is exactly met, and $1500 of the $5500 budget goes unused. The budget isn't what limits the plan; the trip requirement is. The truck-fewer-than-van rule also has room to spare (19 below its limit), so it doesn't restrict the answer either.

Make 25 portions of marinated wild boar and 175 portions of processed lamb chops. This brings in the most revenue possible, $850 per week. Both the 250 minutes of preparation time and the 1,375 ounces of meat are fully used, so they are what limits the plan. The lamb-to-boar requirement has 125 units of slack, meaning the butcher makes more lamb than the minimum that rule requires.

Run the large plant for 40 hours and keep the small plant off (0 hours), which gives the shortest total time of 40 hours. This schedule exactly meets the requirement of 1200 units of water, so the water target is the limiting factor. The by-product requirement is met with 300 units to spare, and 600 filters remain unused, so neither of those limits the schedule. Each extra unit of water required would add about 0.033333 hours to the total.

Schedule **10 cargo ship trips and 6 airplane trips**, which produces the lowest total pollution possible: **410** units. The plan sits exactly at the requirement of at least 6 airplane trips, so that rule is the one that is fully used and it is what forces the airplane count. The rule that at least 750 units be shipped has 10 units of spare capacity, and the rule that ships make up at least 25% of trips has 6 units of slack, so neither is currently limiting the plan. The data don't include shadow prices, so this doesn't show how much the pollution total would change if those limits were loosened.

constraints.name: more truck A than truck B

explanation: The company should send 38 truck A's and 9 truck B's, which collects the most garbage possible: 1,970 units. This plan meets every requirement, including having more truck A's than truck B's. The limit on the plan is the workforce: all 150 workers are needed, so no more trucks can run without hiring. The "more truck A's than truck B's" rule has room to spare (28 units of slack), so it is not what restricts the plan.

The company should schedule **7 expert shifts** and **54 apprentice shifts**, which covers the land at the lowest total cost of **$19,700**. This plan meets all three requirements: it cares for the 5,000 square meters needed, it has at least twice as many apprentice shifts as expert shifts, and expert shifts make up at least 10% of the total. No requirement is exactly met at its limit, so the plan has some room to spare. The land plan covers 20 square meters more than required, and the apprentice-to-expert ratio is 40 shifts above its minimum. The expert share is only 0.9 shifts above its minimum, so it's the closest to its limit. The plan is only as good as the assumed costs, the 100 and 80 square meter care rates, and the three rules, and the model doesn't show how much the cost would change if any of those rules were relaxed.

The best plan is to deliver 50 diabetic pill doses and no diabetic shot doses. This gives the patient 100 units of blood pressure reducing medicine, the most possible under the limits. The stress limit of 20 units is completely used up, so it is what stops the doctor from giving more. The glucose requirement of at least 30 units is exceeded by 20 units, so that requirement is not what is holding the plan back.

Run Method Y 108.3 times and don't run Method X at all. This yields about 75.83 units of the desired element, the most possible with the available materials. Aluminum is the bottleneck: all 650 au is used, and each extra au would add about 0.117 units of output. Oxygen is not the limit, since about 208.3 au of it would go unused.

Use all 6 manual pallet jacks and all 15 electric pallet jacks. Together they move 465 boxes per hour, the most the company can achieve under these rules. Both fleet limits are fully used, so the company's total supply of jacks is what caps the result. The other rules are not holding it back: the manual-use cap has 2 spare, the minimum of 5 electric jacks has 10 spare, and the electric-must-exceed-manual rule has 8 spare. Adding more jacks would be the only way to raise the total, since the model gives no shadow prices to show the value of each extra jack.

Use **4 medium containers and 12 large containers**. This gives the lowest possible total of **44 checks per week**. The rule that large containers must be three times the medium count is the main limit on the plan: it forces the mix and is fully used. The storage requirement is met with 80 units to spare, and the other minimums also have room, so the plan is not stretched to any other limit.

The chemist should run the gamma experiment 100 times and the omega experiment 400 times. This produces 7,600 units of element A, the most possible with the given resources. Electricity and copper are both fully used, so they are what limit the output. The time budget has 300 minutes to spare, so more time alone would not produce more element A.

Allocate all 225 hectares to employee hand-picking and none to U-pick. This yields the maximum of 13,500 lbs of strawberries. The land is the only limit that is fully used: each additional hectare would add about 60 lbs, so more land would help if it could be obtained. Picking time (1,250 minutes) and waste (5,275 lbs) both still have room to spare, so they are not restricting the result at this plan.

The model says the store should make no sofas and no beds, which gives a total shipping time of 0. That result is trivial because the model has no requirement to produce anything, so shipping time is minimized by building nothing. The wood (620) and time (1055) limits are not binding, and the only binding rule is that sofas must equal twice the number of beds, which 0 and 0 satisfy. To get a useful plan, the model would need a minimum production or sales target.

Make 20 diabetic pills and 30 latex gloves. This is the cheapest mix in minutes that meets the rules, and it takes a total of 8.5 minutes of manufacturing time. The limits are the minimum of 20 pills and the rule that gloves must be at least 60% of output, since both are fully used at this solution. The cornstarch supply is not the constraint, with 710 mg left over, so the plan is limited by those two rules rather than by materials.

Make 1 coffee and 2 cappuccinos. This uses 10 units of water, the least the model allows while meeting all the rules. The only constraint fully used is the requirement that cappuccinos outnumber coffees by at least one, and that rule is what limits the mix. Milk (3292 units) and cream (2586 units) have plenty left over, and the 30% coffee rule has 0.1 to spare, so those limits don't restrict the result. As written, the model applies the milk limit only to coffee and the cream limit only to cappuccino, so those leftover figures reflect that setup.

Take 7 servings of super vitamin XYZ and 11 servings of vitamin ABC. This gives the lowest total drowsiness possible under the rules, a total of 47 units. Every requirement is met: vitamin intake exceeds the 30 mg minimum by 0.5 mg, fiber exceeds 55 mg by 13 mg, XYZ makes up less than the 40% limit with room to spare, and you're taking 4 more XYZ servings than the 3-serving minimum. No limit is fully used up, so the plan has some room, but the vitamin target is the closest to its limit. Because all whole-serving amounts are required, the answer is only valid for whole servings, which is what the model enforces.

Contract 4 internal drivers and 12 external drivers. Together they deliver exactly the required 500 routers per day, and the plan produces the lowest total pollution, 108 units. The constraint on delivering 500 routers is fully used, so the plan has no spare delivery capacity, and any drop in driver output would leave the requirement unmet. The internal-driver share rule and the minimum of 5 external drivers both have room to spare (0.8 and 7 units of slack), so they are not what limits the plan.

The plan is to send 5 airplanes and 17 helicopters. Together they carry 515 units, which meets the 500-unit requirement, and they take a total of 320 minutes, the lowest possible under these rules.
